1 Samuel 1: Israel has no king, and the tabernacle stands at Shiloh in the hill country of Ephraim, where Eli is priest. The book covers the move from judges to kings, usually dated to the 11th century BC.
1 Samuel 2: Eli's sons serve as priests at Shiloh and take the best of the sacrifices for themselves (1 Samuel 2:12–17).
1 Samuel 3: The boy Samuel serves at Shiloh when "the word of the LORD was precious in those days" (1 Samuel 3:1). Later all Israel "from Dan even to Beersheba" knows him as a prophet.
1 Samuel 4: Israel fights the Philistines between Ebenezer and Aphek. The Philistines capture the ark and Eli dies at ninety-eight (1 Samuel 4:15).
1 Samuel 5: The ark is carried to the Philistine cities of Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron, three of the five Philistine city-states on the southern coastal plain.
1 Samuel 6: After seven months, the Philistines send the ark on a cart to Bethshemesh, an Israelite town in the Sorek valley, during the wheat harvest.
1 Samuel 7: The ark stays at Kirjathjearim twenty years (1 Samuel 7:2). Samuel judges Israel on a yearly circuit of Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpeh, living at Ramah.
1 Samuel 8: Samuel is old, and his sons judge at Beersheba. The elders come to Ramah and ask for a king "like all the nations" (1 Samuel 8:5).
1 Samuel 9: Saul, a Benjamite from Gibeah, searches for his father's donkeys and meets Samuel in the land of Zuph.
1 Samuel 10: Samuel anoints Saul privately, then the tribes choose him by lot at Mizpeh.
1 Samuel 11: Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabeshgilead, east of the Jordan. After Saul's victory, the kingdom is renewed at Gilgal.
1 Samuel 12: At Gilgal, Samuel speaks to Israel as the kingdom begins. It is the time of wheat harvest (1 Samuel 12:17), when rain was rare.
1 Samuel 13: Saul and Jonathan face the Philistines at Michmash and Geba. Israel has no smiths, because the Philistines controlled ironworking (1 Samuel 13:19–20).
1 Samuel 14: Jonathan and his armourbearer climb between two crags at the pass of Michmash to attack a Philistine garrison.
1 Samuel 15: Saul fights the Amalekites "from Havilah until thou comest to Shur" (1 Samuel 15:7), south of Judah. Samuel goes home to Ramah and does not see Saul again.
1 Samuel 16: Samuel anoints David, Jesse's youngest son, at Bethlehem. David enters Saul's service as a harpist.
1 Samuel 17: Israel and the Philistines face each other across the valley of Elah, on the western approach to Judah's hill country. Goliath comes from Gath.
1 Samuel 18: David becomes a commander in Saul's army and marries Saul's daughter Michal.
1 Samuel 19: Saul tries to kill David, who escapes to Samuel at Naioth in Ramah.
1 Samuel 20: David hides during the new moon feast at Saul's table, and Jonathan warns him with arrows in a field.
1 Samuel 21: David receives holy bread from Ahimelech the priest at Nob, then flees to Achish king of Gath.
1 Samuel 22: David gathers four hundred men at the cave of Adullam and takes his parents to Moab. Saul has the priests of Nob killed.
1 Samuel 23: David rescues Keilah from the Philistines and hides in the wilderness of Ziph and Maon, south of Hebron.
1 Samuel 24: David spares Saul in a cave at Engedi, an oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea.
1 Samuel 25: Samuel dies (1 Samuel 25:1). Nabal shears his sheep at Carmel in Judah, and David marries Abigail.
1 Samuel 26: David spares Saul again in the wilderness of Ziph, at the hill of Hachilah.
1 Samuel 27: David lives among the Philistines for a year and four months, and Achish gives him the town of Ziklag (1 Samuel 27:6–7).
1 Samuel 28: The Philistines gather at Shunem and Saul at Gilboa. Saul consults a medium at Endor.
1 Samuel 29: The Philistine lords gather at Aphek and send David back to Ziklag.
1 Samuel 30: Amalekites burn Ziklag. David pursues them across the brook Besor and recovers everything.
1 Samuel 31: Saul and three sons die on mount Gilboa, above the Jezreel valley. The Philistines fasten their bodies to the wall of Bethshan.
2 Samuel 1: David is at Ziklag when a messenger brings news of Saul's death. He laments Saul and Jonathan.
2 Samuel 2: David is anointed king of Judah at Hebron, while Abner makes Saul's son Ishbosheth king over Israel at Mahanaim, east of the Jordan.
2 Samuel 3: David reigns in Hebron seven years and six months (2 Samuel 2:11). Abner defects to David and is killed by Joab.
2 Samuel 4: Ishbosheth is murdered in his house at Mahanaim.
2 Samuel 5: David is anointed king over all Israel at thirty and takes Jerusalem from the Jebusites, reigning there thirty-three years (2 Samuel 5:4–5). The Tel Dan inscription (9th century BC) mentions the ‘house of David.’
2 Samuel 6: David brings the ark from Baale of Judah (Kirjathjearim) to Jerusalem.
2 Samuel 7: David is living in a cedar house in Jerusalem when he wants to build a house for God. Nathan brings God's promise of a lasting dynasty.
2 Samuel 8: David defeats the Philistines, Moab, Zobah, Damascus, and Edom, placing garrisons in Syria and Edom.
2 Samuel 9: David brings Jonathan's son Mephibosheth from Lodebar to eat at his table in Jerusalem.
2 Samuel 10: David's messengers are shamed by Hanun king of Ammon, leading to war with Ammon and its Syrian allies.
2 Samuel 11: "At the time when kings go forth to battle" (2 Samuel 11:1), in spring, Joab besieges Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, while David stays in Jerusalem.
2 Samuel 12: Nathan confronts David. Rabbah, the Ammonite capital (modern Amman, Jordan), falls to David.
2 Samuel 13: Amnon is killed at a sheepshearing feast at Baalhazor, and Absalom flees to his grandfather the king of Geshur, east of the Sea of Galilee, for three years.
2 Samuel 14: Joab arranges Absalom's return to Jerusalem; Absalom waits two more years to see the king (2 Samuel 14:28).
2 Samuel 15: Absalom proclaims himself king at Hebron, and David flees Jerusalem across the brook Kidron and up the mount of Olives.
2 Samuel 16: At Bahurim, Shimei curses David as he flees. Absalom enters Jerusalem.
2 Samuel 17: David crosses the Jordan to Mahanaim, where Barzillai and others bring him supplies.
2 Samuel 18: Absalom's army is defeated in the wood of Ephraim, east of the Jordan, and Absalom is killed.
2 Samuel 19: David returns from Mahanaim to the Jordan, where Judah meets him at Gilgal.
2 Samuel 20: Sheba son of Bichri leads a revolt and is besieged at Abel of Bethmaachah in the far north.
2 Samuel 21: A three-year famine leads David to the Gibeonites. Saul and Jonathan's bones are buried in Benjamin, at Zelah.
2 Samuel 22: David's song of deliverance, also preserved as Psalm 18, is sung after God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul.
2 Samuel 23: "The last words of David" (2 Samuel 23:1) are followed by a list of his mighty men.
2 Samuel 24: David's census takes nine months and twenty days (2 Samuel 24:8). He buys Araunah's threshingfloor in Jerusalem and builds an altar there.
